claim: A choice question reads its keys, not their descriptions: whatever the planner should weigh about a card must be in the key, which is why the bot writes card notes there.
evidence: Tests before the loop: replayed picks did not change at all when a note was added to the description; Laya took a new weapon in 4 of 6 offers once the key said so.

claim: The decision models judge one concrete option at a time better than they rank many at once, so each goal and each move is its own question.
evidence: Tests before the loop, on replayed states; the bot is built around it.

claim: Words beat numbers: describing a move's cost as 'Tibo would get badly hurt' picks the least damaging move far more often than a percentage.
evidence: Tests before the loop, Laya on 50 replayed states: a move within 2% of the least damaging one 90% of the time with words, 80% with 'would lose N%', 38% with the number alone.

claim: A danger rating tracks how many threats a description lists, not which ones, so a fatal move with a short description can rate safest.
evidence: Tests before the loop: Laya rated a fatal move safest in 4 of 8 replayed states, and stood in hot oil forecast 'very badly hurt' for ten seconds while every step out was 'scratched'. The bot therefore never offers moves the forecast prices clearly worse.

claim: A 0-4 hurt score per move finds the least damaging move more reliably than a yes/no danger question.
evidence: Tests before the loop, Jev on replayed Nightmare steps: 98-100% with the score against 95% with yes/no.

claim: The decision models weigh the start of a text most: what matters goes first.
evidence: Seen while writing the bot's move descriptions; never measured.
